newsitem.title: CHINA: China warns it won't hesitate to rein in markets.
newsitem.headline: China warns it won't hesitate to rein in markets.

text.p: China warned on Wednesday that hopes for a smooth handover of Hong Kong this month would not tie its hands in reining in China's unruly stock markets.
It also advised investors against concluding that all negative news had been wrung out of the market.
"Some investors believed that with the impending return of Hong Kong, the government would not unveil 'bearish' policies to depress the market," said a commentary in the Financial News.
"Obviously, this conclusion is both one-sided and harmful," it said.

"Many investors firmly believed that the market would not fall ahead of the transfer of power and would only reach new highs," the commentary said. "These people have blindly chased stocks prices higher."
Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.

Beijing has been eager to ensure that the historic handover proceeds smoothly. But it also has been concerned that wild fluctuations on the share market would damage its prestige just as world attention focused on the territory, brokers said.

Market regulators have announced a series of measures aimed at calming China's exuberant stock markets, which had surged as much as 50 percent earlier this year before giving up some of those gains recently.
Authorities have announced a sharply expanded quota for new share issues this year in a move that could absorb much of the market's liquidity.
They have raised the stock transaction tax, ordered state banks not to fund stock speculation and most recently told state-run companies to avoid dabbling in the market.

On the nation's biggest stock exchange in the financial centre of Shanghai, the A share index for domestic investors slid 1.71 percent to 1,273.78 on Wednesday after tumbling as much as seven percent earlier in the day.
The negative sentiment spilled over on to the B share market for foreign investors, where the index ended 2.96 percent lower.
Heavy selling also shook the southern bourse in Shenzhen. The domestic A share index tumbled 2.74 percent, dragging down the B share index for foreign investors by 3.22 percent.
The newspaper commentary said the aim of the measures was to regulate rather than depress the market but it noted that the impact would be seen for some time.
"It is unrealistic to believe that at this point all bearish factors have been removed and that the market will stage another big advance in the near future."
